# The Value of Disagreement: Why the Best Meetings Don't End in Consensus

There is a common picture of what a successful meeting looks like: a room full of people who started out with different views and ended up aligned. Someone summarizes the decision, heads nod, and everyone walks out feeling that progress was made. Agreement, in this picture, is the currency of productivity. The meeting worked because the conflict was resolved.

But this picture deserves scrutiny. Agreement is not always what it appears to be. Sometimes it reflects genuine convergence—people heard new arguments and changed their minds. But often it reflects exhaustion, hierarchy, politeness, or the simple desire to leave the room. A meeting can end in unanimous agreement while the underlying disagreement remains fully intact, merely driven underground. The product manager who says "sure, we can ship in March" while privately believing the timeline is fantasy has not agreed to anything. She has simply stopped saying what she thinks. And when March arrives and the product isn't ready, everyone is surprised—except, perhaps, her.

The problem with false agreement is that it hides uncertainty. It takes a question that is still open and makes it look closed. The organization then commits resources, makes promises, and builds plans on top of a foundation
